exampleAnswers.title: Computing a Complement Using a Venn Diagram

question.text:
The Venn diagram shown above represents two events $A$ and $B$ and the number of outcomes in each region of the sample space.

Given that every outcome is equally likely, find $P(B').$
question.explanation:
To calculate the probability of an event using a Venn diagram, we count the number of outcomes in the region that represents the event, and divide by the total number of outcomes of the sample space $\mathcal S.$

In the Venn diagram, $B'$ is represented by the area outside the circle $B$ (see the illustration below).

We count up the outcomes:

  • The number of outcomes in $B'$ is \[ 12+30=42. \]

  • The total number of outcomes in $\mathcal S$ is \[ 12+9+23+30=74. \]

So, we have \[ P(B')=\dfrac{42}{74}=\dfrac{21}{37}. \]

question.text:
The Venn diagram shown above represents two events $A$ and $B$ and the number of outcomes in each region of the sample space.

Given that every outcome is equally likely, find $P\left(A\cap B'\right).$
question.explanation:
To calculate the probability of an event using a Venn diagram, we count the number of outcomes in the region that represents the event, and divide by the total number of outcomes of the sample space $\mathcal S.$

In the Venn diagram, $A\cap B'$ is represented by the area inside the circle $A$ without the intersection between the circles (see the illustration below).

We count up the outcomes:

  • The number of outcomes in $A\cap B'$ is $32.$

  • The total number of outcomes in $\mathcal S$ is \[ 32+22+42+50=146. \]

So, we have \[ P\left(A\cap B'\right)=\dfrac{32}{146}=\dfrac{16}{73}. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Computing a Probability Given a Description of a Sample Space

question.text: An optician registered $80$ customers last week. Of the customers he registered, $55$ purchased corrective glasses, $32$ purchased sunglasses, and $18$ purchased both types of glasses. Draw a Venn diagram representing this sample space. If a customer is selected at random among the $80$ customers, what is the probability that the customer purchased neither corrective glasses nor sunglasses? Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Let us call $A$ the event "customer purchased corrective glasses" and $B$ the event "customer purchased sunglasses."

Note that there are $18$ customers that bought both types of glasses. We draw two overlapping circles representing the events $A$ and $B$ and write the number $18$ where the circles overlap.

  • The number of customers that bought only corrective glasses is \[ 55 - 18= 37, \] so we write the number $37$ in the part of circle $A$ that does not overlap with circle $B.$

  • The number of customers that bought only sunglasses is \[ 32 - 18 = 14, \] so we write the number $14$ in the part of circle $B$ that does not overlap with circle $A.$

The total number of customers that bought corrective glasses or sunglasses is \[ 18+37+14 = 69, \] and there are $80$ customers in total, so the number of remaining customers is \[ 80 - 69 = 11. \]

To represent these $11$ customers that purchased neither corrective glasses nor sunglasses, we write the number $11$ outside of the circles $A$ and $B.$

Therefore, our Venn diagram looks as shown below:

The shaded part of the Venn diagram corresponds to customers that purchased neither corrective glasses nor sunglasses. The probability that a randomly selected student is from this group is given by

\[ P\left(A'\cap B'\right)=\dfrac{11}{80}\approx 0.14, \] rounded to $2$ decimal places.

example.title: Computing a Probability Given a Description of a Sample Space

question.text: At a wedding, the guests may have ice cream or custard with their dessert. There are $80$ guests at the wedding. It was found that $35$ guests prefer ice cream, $38$ guests custard, and $10$ prefer both. Draw a Venn diagram representing this sample space. If a person is selected at random among the $80$ guests, what is the probability that they prefer ice cream but not custard with dessert? Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Let us call $A$ the event "the guest prefers ice cream with dessert" and $B$ the event "the guest prefers custard with dessert."

Note that there are $10$ people who prefer both. We draw two overlapping circles representing the events $A$ and $B$ and write the number $10$ where the circles overlap.

  • The number of people who prefer only ice cream with dessert is \[ 35 - 10 = 25, \] so we write the number $25$ in the part of circle $A$ that does not overlap with circle $B.$

  • The number of people who prefer only custard with dessert is \[ 38 - 10 = 28, \] so we write the number $28$ in the part of the circle $B$ that does not overlap with circle $A.$

The total number of guests who prefer either an ice cream or a custard with dessert is \[ 10 + 25 + 28 = 63, \] and there are $80$ people in total, so the number of remaining people is \[ 80 - 63 = 17. \]

To represent these $17$ people who do not prefer ice cream or custard, we write the number $17$ outside of the circles $A$ and $B.$

Therefore, our Venn diagram looks as shown below:

The shaded part of the Venn diagram corresponds to people who prefer ice cream but not custard with dessert. The probability that a randomly selected person is from this group is given by

\[ P\left(A\cap B'\right)=\dfrac{25}{80}\approx 0.31, \] rounded to $2$ decimal places.

example.title: Computing a Probability Given a Description of a Sample Space

question.text: A class has $76$ students. Of the students, $35$ of them study mathematics, $26$ of them study physics. There are $12$ students that study mathematics and physics. Draw a Venn diagram representing this sample space. If a student is selected at random among the $76$ students, what is the probability that the student studies neither mathematics nor physics? Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Let us call $A$ the event "the student studies mathematics" and $B$ the event "the student studies physics."

Note that there are $12$ students who study both mathematics and physics. So, we draw two overlapping circles representing the events $A$ and $B$ and write the number $12$ where the circles overlap.

  • The number of students who study mathematics only is \[ 35 - 12 = 23, \] so we write the number $23$ in the part of circle $A$ that does not overlap with circle $B.$

  • The number of students who study physics only is \[ 26 - 12 = 14, \] so we write the number $14$ in the part of the circle $B$ that does not overlap with circle $A.$

The total number of students who study mathematics or physics is \[ 12 + 23 + 14 = 49, \] and there are $76$ students in total, so the number of remaining students is \[ 76 - 49 = 27. \]

To represent these $27$ students who do not study mathematics nor physics, we write the number $27$ outside of the circles $A$ and $B.$

Therefore, our Venn diagram looks as shown below:

The shaded part of the Venn diagram corresponds to students that don't study mathematics or physics. The probability that a randomly selected student is from this group is given by

\[ P\left(A'\cap B'\right)=\dfrac{27}{76}\approx 0.36, \] rounded to $2$ decimal places.

example.title: Computing a Probability Given a Description of a Sample Space

question.text: In a survey conducted among $100$ people, it was found that $38\%$ of them have been in Canada, $70\%$ have been in France, and $11\%$ have been in both countries. Draw a Venn diagram representing this sample space. If a person is selected at random among the $100$ people, what is the probability that he has been in Canada but not in France? Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Clearly, $38$ people have been in Canada, $70$ people have been in France, and $11$ people have been to both countries.

Let us call $C$ the event "the person has been in Canada" and $F$ the event "the person has been in France."

Note that there are $11$ people who have been in both countries. We draw two overlapping circles representing the events $C$ and $F$ and write the number $11$ where the circles overlap.

  • The number of people who have been in Canada only is \[ 38- 11 = 27, \] so we write the number $27$ in the part of circle $C$ that does not overlap with circle $F.$

  • The number of people who have been in France only is \[ 70 - 11 =59, \] so we write the number $59$ in the part of circle $F$ that does not overlap with circle $C.$

The total number of people who have been in Canada or France is \[ 27+11+59 = 97, \] and there are $100$ people in total, so the number of remaining people is \[ 100-97 =3. \]

To represent these $3$ people who have not been in Canada or France, we write the number $3$ outside of the circles $C$ and $F.$

Therefore, our Venn diagram looks as shown below:

The shaded part of the Venn diagram corresponds to people that have been to Canada but not in France. The probability that a randomly selected person is from this group is given by

\[ P\left(C\cap F'\right)=\dfrac{27}{100}=0.27. \]
